1. Core Clinical Tension: A 21-year-old Japanese male with a childhood ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt presents with high fever, acute abdominal distension, worsening headache, and obtundation. Triage imaging reveals acute hydrocephalus and a giant abdominal pseudocyst surrounding the distal shunt catheter, highly mimicking acute pyogenic bacterial shunt infection/peritonitis. However, sterile fluid cultures, lack of typical bacterial response to broad-spectrum antibiotics, and subsequent knee monoarthritis reveal extrapulmonary peritoneal tuberculosis in a patient from a non-endemic, low-incidence nation without pulmonary signs.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint falls immediately after physical examination and initial emergency department imaging/laboratories (CBC, CRP, plain chest radiograph, brain CT, and abdominal CT showing enlarged ventricles and the giant abdominal cyst), strictly prior to external surgical shunt drainage, pseudocyst aspiration, and operative interventions.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute pyogenic bacterial shunt infection/peritonitis is the most frequent cause of shunt malfunction and abdominal pseudocyst, but repeated bacterial cultures are sterile and antibiotics fail to halt pseudocyst recollection. Peritoneal neoplasm/omental carcinomatosis is ruled out by negative peritoneal cytology and benign exploratory laparotomy. Tuberculous peritonitis with shunt malfunction is definitively confirmed when knee monoarthritis develops and synovial fluid culture isolates Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
case_prompt:
A 21-year-old Japanese male presents with a two-month history of sporadic nausea, a one-month history of abdominal discomfort, and progressive severe headaches. During infancy (at 11 months of age), he had cysto-peritoneal (CP) and ventriculo-peritoneal (VP) shunts implanted for hydrocephalus secondary to a suprasellar arachnoid cyst. His VP shunt had been revised twice by age 13; at his last revision, the CP cranial catheter was removed while the extracranial tube was left in situ as it traversed the mediastinum. He has lived with slit ventricle syndrome but has maintained normal daily activities with mild cognitive impairment. He has no prior history of chronic systemic illnesses or infectious exposures and has never traveled abroad.

A few days prior to presentation, he developed high fevers and progressive lethargy with mild disturbance of consciousness. On physical examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.9°C and exhibits restlessness. Abdominal examination reveals prominent abdominal distension with diffuse discomfort. There is no neck stiffness or signs of meningeal irritation, and no focal cranial or motor neurological deficits are present.

Emergency laboratory testing reveals a white blood cell count of 10,900/mm³ and a markedly elevated serum C-reactive protein of 31.8 mg/dL. A plain chest radiograph is normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain shows enlargement of the lateral ventricles indicative of acute shunt obstruction and increased intracranial pressure. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen reveals a massive peritoneal fluid collection surrounding the distal tip of the peritoneal shunt catheter, along with fluid tracking in the subcutaneous sheath surrounding the catheter. A chest CT scan shows normal bilateral lung parenchyma and clear mediastinal structures.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Pyogenic Bacterial Shunt Infection / Bacterial Peritonitis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute high fever, severe abdominal distension, markedly elevated CRP (31.8 mg/dL), and a huge abdominal fluid collection surrounding a VP shunt catheter initially raised strong suspicion for common pyogenic bacterial colonization (such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, S. aureus, or Enterobacteriaceae); however, repeated aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cultures of both CSF and cyst fluid remained sterile, and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic regimens failed to resolve inflammation or prevent rapid fluid re-accumulation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Antibiotic therapies for abdominal infection were empirically administered and bacterial cultures analyzed, but no causative pathogen was identified... However, the cyst fluid gradually recollected and signs of mild inflammation remained despite antibiotic therapy.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Peritoneal Malignancy / Carcinomatosis / True Intra-abdominal Cystic Neoplasm
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A massive, non-resolving intra-abdominal fluid collection with marked systemic inflammatory markers raised concern for omental carcinomatosis, pseudomyxoma peritonei, or an uncharacterized intra-abdominal malignancy; ruled out by multiple negative cytological examinations and exploratory laparotomy demonstrating a fibrous, unlined pseudocyst without omental implants, true cyst wall, or ascites.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In the third stage of treatment, laparotomy was performed, which revealed no membrane surrounding the abdominal cyst (defining it as a pseudocyst), no malignancies within the omentum, and no ascites within the abdominal cavity. Throughout the course of treatment, all cytological examinations for malignancies were negative

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Peritoneal Tuberculosis Presenting as VP Shunt Malfunction
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnosis of peritoneal tuberculosis remained elusive until two months after presentation, when the patient developed acute left knee monoarthritis yielding xanthochromatic synovial fluid identical in appearance to the abdominal pseudocyst fluid, which grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis on mycobacterial culture. Institution of antituberculous chemotherapy and conversion to a ventriculopleural shunt resulted in complete clinical recovery.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Two months after initial surgery, inflammation of his left knee joint became apparent. The fluid taken from the joint was xanthochromatic, similar to the pseudocyst fluid, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis was detected in a culture from the fluid. Thus, the patient was diagnosed with an abdominal pseudocyst associated with TBP and successfully treated by anti-TB agents following insertion of a ventriculo-pleural shunt [Figure 3].

editor_comments: Breakpoint established before invasive shunt drainage and laparotomy. Prompt provides clinical, lab, and radiological findings while excluding pathogen and culture data.
